newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan appointed U.N. secretary-general from Jan 1.
newsitem.headline: Annan appointed U.N. secretary-general from Jan 1.

text.p: Kofi Annan, a 58-year-old U.N. career official from Ghana, was appointed by the General Assembly by acclamation on Tuesday to a five-year term as secretary-general of the United Nations, beginning January 1, 1997.
Annan, currently undersecretary-general for peacekeeping operations, will be the seventh secretary-general in the history of the 51-year-old organisation.
He will also be the first from sub-Saharan Africa and the first to have risen through the ranks of the U.N. bureaucracy.
The 15-member Security Council nominated Annan last Friday to the $205,809-a-year post, making his appointment by the 185-nation Assembly a formality.

He will succeed the 74-year-old Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, to whom the Assembly paid tribute in another resolution adopted by acclamation but whose hopes for a second term as secretary-general were blocked by a United States veto.
Washington said he had not done enough to carry out reforms and that the world organisation needed new leadership.

Boutros-Ghali's predecessor as secretary-general, Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, was among those attending the gala ceremony in the gold and blue Assembly hall, chaired by Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia wearing national dress.

After the Assembly adopted the resolution appointing Annan, the Ghanaian diplomat, wearing a dark gray business suit, was ushered into the hall by the U.N. chief of protocol and shook hands warmly with Boutros-Ghali.

The outgoing secretary-general, in his last address to the Assembly, delivered a thinly veiled jab at the United States for its U.N. arrears of some $1.3 billion to the world body and defended the independence of his office.
The financial crisis was "not the result of mismanagement," he said, rejecting a charge often levelled at him.

"It is the refusal to fulfil a treaty obligation. Now that a new secretary-general is being appointed, all arrears should be paid at once, as has been promised so often in the past few months," he added pointedly as U.S. ambassador Madeleine Albright, seated at the head of her delegation, looked on stonily.

Boutros-Ghali, who delivered sections of speech in English, Arabic and French, outlined some of the United Nations' achivements of his five year term, including peacemaking, peacekeeping, development and democratization.
In that time the organisation had passed through periods of enthusiasm, disillusion, and then realism, he said. "Now let us look to the future."
If one word was to characterise a secretary-general it was independence, Boutros-Ghali said.
"The holder of this office must never be seen as acting out of fear, or in an attempt to curry favour, with one state or group of states," he declared.
"Should that happen, all prospects for the United Nations would be lost."

And, in a possible rebuttal of the oft-repeated U.S. assertion that a secretary-general's first thoughts should focus on reform, he added: "Throughout the past five years, the first thing I though of when I awoke in the morning were my responsibilities as secretary-general to the ideal of the Charter and independence and credibility of the organisation."
